newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-MUSTER TAPS IN TO COMPUTER TO SPY ON RIVALS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-MUSTER TAPS IN TO COMPUTER TO SPY ON RIVALS.

text.p: Austrian Thomas Muster's avant-garde approach to tennis involves throwing a medicine ball around for hours on end, using a longer racket, and strapping his recuperating body into a chair so he can train.
On Wednesday, he revealed a new weapon: a computer.
Fifth-seeded Muster stormed into the semifinals of the Australian Open at Melbourne Park by neutralising Goran Ivanisevic's lethal serve to triumph 6-4 6-2 6-3.
Asked by a reporter if he knew what was coming, Muster said: "Yeah, my coach figured it out. We had a computer and we did it with the computer.
"I had a good concept going in there and I tried to read his serve...I really tried to figure out where the strong parts of his serve were."

"I play tactically not so smart," acknowledged Ivanisevic. "I wanted to come in so far because he is standing too far back and I thought maybe when I hit a first serve then come in, but every time I came in I hit volleys everywhere."
Muster, who briefly rose to world number one in the world rankings last year, said his coach had developed a computer programme on all the top players.
Ivanisevic, obviously distressed by Muster's ability to read his serve, managed to hit the mark with only 39 percent of his first serves, dipping to 20 percent in the third set.

"Since we are using technology with rackets, we are taking advantage of so many other things in tennis, I think that statistics are very important," said Muster, who started using a longer racket at the end of last year.
"It (a computer) can help you, but it's never going to do the work for you on court."
Muster, who has only dropped one set in five matches, has been dismissed by some tennis purists for only displaying his best form on clay -- a charge he rejects.
Forty of the Austrian's 42 career titles have been won on clay. On the grass at Wimbledon he has never won a match.
Muster said he trains by throwing medicine balls for "as long as the match lasts".
The Austrian is a fitness fanatic and, following surgery after an accident in 1989, had a special chair designed so he could practice hitting balls.
"It is pretty strange," said Ivanisevic. "I am sitting on the changeover and he is already waiting for me to serve.
"I said, 'Jesus what is going here', but that's him, you know, that's how he plays it, it is tough mentally.
"Nobody is like Thomas...if you want to beat him you have to be tough, it is not easy."
Ivanisevic believes Muster, who meets world number one Pete Sampras in Friday's semifinal, will go on to win only his second grand slam title.
"This is not a very fast court and I think he has a good game to beat Pete...and if he beats Pete he is going to win the tournament pretty easily," he said.
